mcqs.question: Which of the following is a RAW hazard?
options: Instruction B writes a register that instruction A, issued earlier, still needs to read
Instruction B needs to read a register that instruction A, issued earlier, hasn't written yet
Two instructions both write the same register, and the wrong one's write ends up 'winning'
Two instructions both try to read the register file in the same cycle
mcqs.explanation: RAW (read-after-write) is exactly this: a later instruction needs to read a value an earlier instruction produces, before that value is actually written. The other options describe WAR (option 1, worded backwards) and WAW (option 3) hazards, which can't occur in a simple in-order pipeline; option 4 is not a hazard at all in single-ported read designs since reads don't conflict with each other.

mcqs.question: Why can't WAR or WAW hazards occur in a simple in-order 5-stage pipeline?
options: Because the register file only has one write port
Because instructions reach every stage in strict program order, so a later instruction can never write before an earlier one reads or writes the same register
Because forwarding prevents them automatically
Because compilers never generate code that could trigger them
mcqs.explanation: In-order execution means every instruction proceeds through the pipeline stages in the same order it was issued, so a later instruction physically cannot overtake an earlier one's read or write — the precondition for WAR/WAW simply never arises. This has nothing to do with the register file's port count, forwarding, or compiler behavior; it only becomes possible once execution goes out of order.

mcqs.question: What does forwarding actually do to resolve a RAW hazard between two back-to-back ALU instructions?
options: It stalls the second instruction until the first reaches write-back
It routes the first instruction's result directly from its pipeline register to the second instruction's ALU input, bypassing the register file
It reorders the two instructions so the dependency disappears
It duplicates the ALU so both instructions compute independently
mcqs.explanation: Forwarding adds a direct wire from the producing instruction's pipeline register (e.g. EX/MEM) straight into the consuming instruction's ALU input, so the value is available the same cycle it's needed without waiting for write-back and a register-file read. It doesn't stall, reorder instructions, or need a duplicated ALU.

mcqs.question: Why can't forwarding alone eliminate the load-use hazard the way it eliminates ALU-to-ALU RAW hazards?
options: Loads don't produce a value that can be forwarded at all
A load's result isn't available until the end of MEM, one stage later than an ALU result, so it can't reach a dependent instruction's EX stage in time
Forwarding hardware is physically incompatible with load instructions
The register file blocks forwarding for any load-produced value
mcqs.explanation: An ALU instruction's result is ready at the end of EX, exactly when the next instruction needs it in its own EX stage. A load's result isn't ready until the end of MEM — one stage later — so even forwarding as fast as hardware allows still arrives one cycle after a dependent instruction's EX stage would need it, forcing one stall cycle.

mcqs.question: In the LW/ADD example, exactly how many stall cycles does hardware need to insert?
options: Zero — forwarding alone handles it
One
Two
It depends on which register is used
mcqs.explanation: The gap between when a load's value is ready (end of MEM) and when a back-to-back dependent instruction would need it (its own EX stage) is exactly one cycle, so hardware inserts exactly one bubble and then forwards the value from MEM/WB into the now-delayed EX stage. It isn't zero (forwarding alone can't close a full stage gap) or two (only one stage separates the two timings), and it doesn't depend on which register is used.
